title: The Second Markale Massacre: The Trigger for Deliberate Force
sources: ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T), second Markale incident
content:
On the morning of 28 August 1995, a single 120mm mortar round struck the Markale marketplace in central Sarajevo, killing forty-three people and wounding approximately seventy-five others. It was the second mass-casualty shelling to hit the same market during the siege — the first, in February 1994, had killed sixty-eight and prompted a NATO ultimatum that temporarily restrained Bosnian Serb heavy weapons around the city. This time, the international response would be decisive.

The Markale marketplace occupied a narrow street in the old commercial district of Sarajevo, an area that remained one of the few functioning civilian gathering points in a city that had been under continuous siege since April 1992. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, by then commanded by General Dragomir Milošević (whose own case, IT-98-29/1-T, would address this period of the siege) of the VRS maintained artillery and mortar positions on the ridgelines surrounding the city, from which it had conducted a sustained bombardment campaign that the ICTY, in its judgment against General Stanislav Galić (IT-98-29-T), characterized as a campaign of terror against the civilian population. The second Markale shelling fit the pattern of attacks directed at locations where civilians were known to congregate.

UNPROFOR crater analysis conducted immediately after the attack determined that the round had been fired from Bosnian Serb positions. The Bosnian Serb leadership denied responsibility and alleged, as it had after the first Markale incident, that the Bosnian government had staged the attack against its own population. These claims were investigated and rejected by UN technical teams. The ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T) addressed the second Markale massacre within its broader findings on the Sarajevo siege, concluding that the mortar fire originated from VRS-held territory.

The political significance of the second Markale massacre far exceeded its immediate human toll, grievous as that was. The shelling occurred at a moment when international patience with the Bosnian Serb leadership had been exhausted by the fall of Srebrenica and Žepa, and when NATO military planning for a sustained air campaign had already been advanced. The marketplace attack provided the immediate catalyst. On 30 August 1995, NATO launched Operation Deliberate Force — a sustained bombing campaign against Bosnian Serb military targets, command infrastructure, and communications networks across Bosnia.

Deliberate Force lasted until 14 September 1995 and involved approximately 3,500 sorties by aircraft from multiple NATO nations. It targeted ammunition depots, radar installations, command bunkers, and communications facilities, systematically degrading the VRS capacity to coordinate military operations. The campaign, combined with the territorial losses inflicted by the Croatian-Bosnian ground offensive in western Bosnia, fundamentally altered the military balance that had sustained the war for three years.

The connection between the Markale shelling and the initiation of Deliberate Force was not merely sequential but structural. NATO had established conditions under which a mass-casualty attack on a Safe Area would trigger an air response, but the political will to act on those conditions had been absent through years of siege and atrocity. The cumulative weight of Srebrenica, Žepa, and now a second marketplace massacre finally collapsed the distinction between threat and action. Within weeks, the parties were at the negotiating table. The Dayton proximity talks began on 1 November 1995. The second Markale shelling was, in the war's grim arithmetic, the last atrocity the international community was willing to absorb before intervening with force sufficient to end the conflict.
